stimuli.title: Nitrogen Fertilizer and Corn Growth
stimuli.html:
An agriculture student planted 20 corn seedlings of the same variety in 20 identical pots filled with the same soil. She divided the pots into four groups of 5. Once a week for 5 weeks, each pot received a set amount of nitrogen fertilizer dissolved in 500 mL of water. All pots were kept in the same greenhouse, at the same temperature, and received the same amount of light. At the end of 5 weeks, she measured the height of every plant.

Fertilizer per week (g)Plant 1Plant 2Plant 3Plant 4Plant 5Mean height (cm)
0404441434242
2545753565555
46366616862?
8505349525151

All heights are in centimeters. She also noted that the leaf tips of the plants in the 8 g group had turned brown and dry.

stimuli.title: Kernel Color in Corn
stimuli.html:
Each kernel on an ear of corn develops from a separately fertilized ovule, so every kernel is a separate offspring with its own genotype. In one type of corn, the allele for purple kernels (P) is dominant over the allele for yellow kernels (p).

A plant breeder crossed two corn plants whose genotypes were not recorded. One ear from this cross had 312 purple kernels and 104 yellow kernels.

stimuli.title: Feeding Relationships in a Wheat Field
stimuli.html:
The list below describes feeding relationships in and around a wheat field. Each arrow means "is eaten by."

  • Wheat → aphids
  • Wheat → grasshoppers
  • Wheat seeds → field mice
  • Aphids → ladybugs
  • Grasshoppers → meadowlarks
  • Ladybugs → meadowlarks
  • Field mice → hawks
  • Meadowlarks → hawks

Aphids are small insects that suck sap from wheat plants and can greatly reduce a farmer's harvest. A single ladybug can eat about 50 aphids per day. Some farmers now plant strips of wildflowers along the edges of their fields. The flowers provide nectar, pollen, and shelter that help ladybugs and other aphid-eating insects survive and reproduce. Farmers who use flower strips often need to spray less insecticide.

stimuli.title: Leaves in Dry Weather
stimuli.html:
The surface of a leaf has thousands of tiny pores called stomata, most of them on the underside. Carbon dioxide from the air enters the leaf through the stomata, and water vapor escapes from the leaf through the same openings. Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells, which swell to open the pore and shrink to close it.

During hot, dry weather, many crop plants close their stomata for much of the day. This helps the plant hold on to water when the soil is dry, but it also limits how much gas can move into and out of the leaf.

stimuli.title: Lifting Grain into a Storage Bin
stimuli.html:
On a grain farm, a motor-driven bucket elevator lifts harvested grain to the top of a storage bin. In one test, the elevator lifted grain weighing a total of 1,500 newtons (N) straight up a height of 12 meters (m) in 30 seconds (s).

Work is found with W = F × d, where F is force in newtons and d is distance in meters. Work is measured in joules (J). Power is found with P = W ÷ t, where t is time in seconds. Power is measured in watts (W); 1 watt = 1 joule per second.

stimuli.title: Soil pH and Crops
stimuli.html:
A farmer tested the soil in four fields. Crops grow best when soil pH is within a certain range. On the pH scale, 7 is neutral, values below 7 are acidic, and values above 7 are basic.

FieldSoil pH
A5.2
B6.5
C7.0
D8.1
CropBest soil pH range
Blueberries4.5 to 5.5
Potatoes5.8 to 6.5
Corn5.8 to 7.0
Alfalfa6.5 to 7.5

To change soil pH, farmers can spread ground limestone (calcium carbonate), which is a base, or elemental sulfur, which soil bacteria slowly convert into an acid.

stimuli.title: Making Ammonia for Fertilizer
stimuli.html:
Most nitrogen fertilizer used on farms begins as ammonia (NH3). Factories make ammonia by reacting nitrogen gas (N2) from the air with hydrogen gas (H2) at high temperature and pressure. The unbalanced equation for the reaction is:

N2 + H2 → NH3

stimuli.title: Protecting Crops from Frost
stimuli.html:
When a freezing night is forecast, strawberry and citrus growers sometimes turn on sprinklers and spray water over their plants all night. As the water on the plants freezes, it releases heat, about 334 joules for every gram of water that turns to ice. As long as fresh water keeps freezing on the plants, this released heat keeps the plant tissue at about 0 °C, even when the air around it is several degrees colder. Most crop damage begins only when plant tissue drops below about −2 °C.

Frost is most likely on clear, calm nights. After sunset, the ground and plants lose heat by giving off infrared radiation toward the sky. Clouds absorb some of this radiation and send part of it back toward the ground.

stimuli.title: A Hay Delivery Trip
stimuli.html:
A truck carried a load of hay from a farm to a livestock auction. The truck stopped once along the way at a farm supply store. The graph and table show the truck's distance from the farm during the first hour of the trip.

Time (min)0102030405060
Distance from farm (km)0122424243852

figure.title: Distance of Hay Truck from Farm

items.prompt: Which hypothesis was the student most likely testing?
options: The amount of nitrogen fertilizer given to corn plants affects how tall they grow.
Corn plants grow taller in a greenhouse than in an outdoor field.
Corn plants grow taller when they are watered more often.
Different varieties of corn grow to different heights.
items.explain:
The only factor the student changed from group to group was the amount of nitrogen fertilizer (0, 2, 4, or 8 g per week), and she measured plant height. So her hypothesis must connect fertilizer amount to height.

All plants were grown in the same greenhouse and given the same 500 mL of water, so the experiment cannot test indoor versus outdoor growth or watering. All seedlings were the same variety, so variety was not tested either.

items.prompt: Which group served as the control group in this experiment?
options: The group that received 4 g of fertilizer, because it grew the tallest
The group that received 8 g of fertilizer, because it received the most
The group that received no fertilizer
All 20 pots, because they all received the same amount of water
items.explain:
A control group does not receive the treatment being tested, so it gives a baseline for comparison. The 0 g group received no fertilizer, so the other groups can be compared to it.

The 4 g and 8 g groups received the treatment, so they are experimental groups; growing tallest or receiving the most does not make a group the control. Giving every pot the same water makes water a controlled variable, which is different from a control group.

items.prompt: What is the mean height, in centimeters, of the plants that received 4 g of fertilizer per week? Enter a whole number.
items.explain:
Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values.

63 + 66 + 61 + 68 + 62 = 320
320 ÷ 5 = 64 cm

Divide by 5, the number of plants in the group, not by 4 (the number of groups).

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the results?
options: Corn grows taller with every increase in the amount of nitrogen fertilizer.
Nitrogen fertilizer has no effect on the height of corn plants.
The plants that received 8 g of fertilizer per week died before the end of the study.
Mean height increased as fertilizer increased up to 4 g per week, but 8 g per week produced shorter plants than 4 g did.
items.explain:
Mean heights were 42 cm (0 g), 55 cm (2 g), 64 cm (4 g), and 51 cm (8 g). Height rose up to 4 g, then fell at 8 g, and the browned leaf tips suggest that too much fertilizer harmed the plants.

Height did not rise with every increase, because 51 cm is less than 64 cm. Fertilizer clearly had an effect, since every fertilized group was taller than the 42 cm control. Nothing in the results says the 8 g plants died; the student reports only that their leaf tips turned brown and dry, and she measured their heights (49–53 cm) at the end of the study.

items.prompt: Which cross most likely produced the ear of corn described?
options: Homozygous purple (PP) × yellow (pp)
Heterozygous (Pp) × yellow (pp)
Heterozygous (Pp) × heterozygous (Pp)
Homozygous purple (PP) × heterozygous (Pp)
items.explain:
Find the ratio: 312 ÷ 104 = 3, so the ear shows about 3 purple : 1 yellow.

A Pp × Pp cross gives PP, Pp, Pp, and pp: 3 purple to 1 yellow. That matches.

PP × pp and PP × Pp give all purple kernels, because every offspring gets at least one P. Pp × pp gives a 1 : 1 ratio (half purple, half yellow), not 3 : 1.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the kernels on this ear.

Every yellow kernel on the ear has the genotype {{0}}. A purple kernel on the ear could have the genotype {{1}}.

options: homozygous dominant (PP)
heterozygous (Pp)
homozygous recessive (pp)
homozygous dominant (PP) only
heterozygous (Pp) only
either PP or Pp
homozygous recessive (pp)

items.explain:
Yellow is the recessive trait, so it appears only when a kernel has two recessive alleles: pp.

Purple is dominant, so a purple kernel needs just one P. From a Pp × Pp cross, purple kernels can be PP or Pp; their color alone cannot tell which. Choosing "heterozygous (Pp) only" ignores the PP box of the Punnett square.

items.prompt: The breeder grows a plant from one of the purple kernels and crosses it with a plant grown from a yellow kernel (pp). The resulting ear has 240 kernels: 122 purple and 118 yellow. What is the genotype of the plant grown from the purple kernel?
options: PP, because purple is the dominant color
Pp, because about half of the kernels are yellow
pp, because some of the kernels are yellow
PP, because more than half of the kernels are purple
items.explain:
Compare the two possibilities:

  • PP × pp: every offspring gets P from the purple parent, so all kernels would be purple (Pp).
  • Pp × pp: half the offspring get P (Pp, purple) and half get p (pp, yellow), a 1 : 1 ratio.

118 of 240 kernels is about half (118 ÷ 240 ≈ 49%), so the purple parent must be Pp.

A PP parent could not produce any yellow kernels. A pp parent would have yellow kernels itself, but this plant grew from a purple kernel.

items.prompt: Modern corn was developed from a wild grass called teosinte. A teosinte ear is only a few centimeters long and holds about a dozen kernels, each sealed in a hard, stony case. Over thousands of years, farmers in Mexico saved and planted seeds from the plants with the largest ears and the softest kernels. Which process does this description best illustrate?
options: Natural selection, because the environment alone decided which plants survived
Inheritance of acquired traits, because well-cared-for plants passed on the larger ears they developed during their lives
Genetic engineering, because scientists inserted genes for larger ears into teosinte
Selective breeding, because people chose which plants would reproduce based on desired traits
items.explain:
The farmers chose which plants would produce the next generation, based on traits they wanted (large ears, soft kernels). That is selective (artificial) breeding.

In natural selection, the environment, not people, determines which individuals reproduce. Traits a plant develops during its life because of care are not passed on through seeds. Genetic engineering is a modern laboratory method; the passage describes farmers saving seeds over thousands of years.

items.prompt: Use the feeding relationships in the wheat field to classify each living thing. Drag each one into the correct category.
items.explain:
Producer: Wheat makes its own food by photosynthesis.

Primary consumers: Aphids, grasshoppers, and field mice all eat wheat (or its seeds), the producer.

Secondary consumer: Ladybugs eat aphids, which are primary consumers.

A common mistake is calling field mice secondary consumers because hawks eat them. A consumer's level depends on what it eats, and field mice eat wheat seeds.

items.prompt: A new highway is built near the field, and most of the meadowlarks leave the area. Which change in the aphid population is most likely to follow?
options: The aphid population decreases, because more ladybugs survive to eat aphids.
The aphid population increases, because meadowlarks no longer eat aphids.
The aphid population stays the same, because meadowlarks do not eat aphids.
The aphid population increases, because hawks begin eating ladybugs instead of meadowlarks.
items.explain:
Follow the chain: meadowlarks eat ladybugs. With fewer meadowlarks, more ladybugs survive. Ladybugs eat aphids, so more ladybugs means fewer aphids.

Meadowlarks do not eat aphids, so their loss cannot directly increase aphids. But "stays the same" ignores the indirect effect through ladybugs; a change at one level can affect organisms that are not directly connected. Hawks are not listed as eating ladybugs.

items.prompt:
Based on the passage, how do wildflower strips help farmers spray less insecticide?

Select two answers.
options: The flowers give ladybugs food and shelter, so more ladybugs survive and reproduce.
Larger ladybug populations eat more aphids, so aphids do less damage to the wheat.
The flowers make the wheat plants produce their own insecticide.
The flowers attract field mice, which eat the aphids.
The flowers shade the wheat, so grasshoppers cannot find it.
items.explain:
The passage says the flowers provide nectar, pollen, and shelter that help ladybugs survive and reproduce, and a ladybug can eat about 50 aphids a day. So more ladybugs means fewer aphids and less damage, which reduces the need to spray.

Nothing in the passage says flowers cause wheat to make insecticide, says field mice eat aphids (they eat wheat seeds), or says flowers hide wheat from grasshoppers.

items.prompt: During a drought, corn leaves droop and curl. The sentences below describe parts of a plant cell. Click the sentence that describes the structure whose loss of water most directly causes the leaves to droop.
spans: The cell wall is a rigid layer outside the cell membrane that gives the cell its shape.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which captures light energy used to make glucose.
The large central vacuole fills with water and presses outward against the cell wall, keeping the cell firm.
Mitochondria release energy stored in glucose.
The nucleus contains DNA that directs the cell's activities.
items.explain:
When the soil is dry, the central vacuole loses water and stops pressing against the cell wall. The cells go limp, and the leaves droop (wilt).

The cell wall gives shape, but it is stiff on its own; the push from a water-filled vacuole is what keeps the cell firm. Chloroplasts, mitochondria, and the nucleus do not hold the water that keeps a plant upright.

items.prompt: During a long drought, a corn plant keeps its stomata closed for most of the day. Which effect is most likely?
options: Its rate of photosynthesis increases, because more water stays inside the plant.
It takes in extra carbon dioxide through its roots to make up the difference.
Its rate of photosynthesis decreases, because less carbon dioxide enters its leaves.
It releases more oxygen, because closed stomata trap carbon dioxide inside the leaf.
items.explain:
Photosynthesis needs carbon dioxide, and the passage says carbon dioxide enters the leaf through the stomata. With the stomata closed, less carbon dioxide enters, so photosynthesis slows.

Saving water helps the plant survive, but it does not speed up photosynthesis when carbon dioxide is limited. Plants take in carbon dioxide through their leaves, not their roots. Less photosynthesis means less oxygen is produced, not more.

items.prompt: When a farmworker's body temperature rises, sweat glands release sweat onto the skin. As the sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from the body. Health experts warn that heat illness is more likely on hot days when the air is also very humid. Which statement best explains why?
options: Humid air contains less oxygen, so the body produces more heat.
Sweat glands stop releasing sweat when the air is humid.
Humid air is always hotter than dry air.
Sweat evaporates more slowly in humid air, so less heat is carried away from the skin.
items.explain:
Sweating cools the body only when the sweat evaporates. Humid air already holds a lot of water vapor, so sweat evaporates slowly and removes less heat. Body temperature can then keep rising.

Sweat glands keep working in humid air; the sweat simply drips instead of evaporating. Humid air is not always hotter than dry air, and the problem is not a shortage of oxygen.

items.prompt: How much work, in joules, did the elevator do on the grain in this test?
items.explain:
W = F × d
W = 1,500 N × 12 m = 18,000 J

The time (30 s) is not used to find work; it is needed only for power. Dividing 1,500 by 12 (125) is a common error.

items.prompt: What was the power output of the elevator during the test?
items.explain:
First find the work: W = 1,500 N × 12 m = 18,000 J.

Then P = W ÷ t = 18,000 J ÷ 30 s = 600 W.

50 W comes from dividing the force by the time (1,500 ÷ 30) without first finding the work. 1,500 W comes from dividing the work by the distance instead of the time. 540,000 W comes from multiplying the work by the time instead of dividing.

items.prompt: Which field's soil is best suited for growing blueberries without any treatment?
options: Field A
Field B
Field C
Field D
items.explain:
Blueberries grow best at pH 4.5 to 5.5. Only Field A (pH 5.2) falls in that range.

Field B (6.5) and Field C (7.0) are too close to neutral, and Field D (8.1) is basic. Blueberries need fairly acidic soil.

items.prompt: The farmer wants to grow alfalfa in Field A. Which action would make the soil in Field A better suited for alfalfa?
options: Add sulfur to raise the pH
Add sulfur to lower the pH
Add limestone to lower the pH
Add limestone to raise the pH
items.explain:
Alfalfa grows best at pH 6.5 to 7.5, but Field A has a pH of 5.2, which is too acidic. The farmer needs to raise the pH. Limestone is a base, and adding a base to acidic soil neutralizes some of the acid, so limestone raises the pH.

Sulfur forms an acid in the soil, so it lowers the pH, the wrong direction for Field A. Limestone does not lower pH, because it is a base.

items.prompt:
Choose the coefficients that balance the equation for making ammonia.

N2 + {{0}} H2 → {{1}} NH3
items.explain:
Start with nitrogen: N2 has 2 nitrogen atoms, so the product side needs 2 NH3.

2 NH3 contains 2 × 3 = 6 hydrogen atoms. Each H2 has 2 hydrogen atoms, so the reactant side needs 3 H2 (3 × 2 = 6).

Check: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 has 2 N and 6 H on each side. Writing N2 + H2 → 2NH3 balances nitrogen but leaves only 2 H on the left and 6 H on the right.

items.prompt: In a test, 70 g of nitrogen gas reacted completely with hydrogen gas, and 85 g of ammonia formed. No other products formed. How many grams of hydrogen gas reacted?
items.explain:
By the law of conservation of mass, the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products.

mass of N2 + mass of H2 = mass of NH3
70 g + mass of H2 = 85 g
mass of H2 = 85 − 70 = 15 g

Adding the two numbers (155 g) is a common error; the 85 g of ammonia already includes the mass of both reactants.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains how spraying water protects the plants on a freezing night?
options: The ice absorbs heat from the plants as it forms, which cools them evenly.
As water freezes on the plants, it releases heat that keeps the plant tissue near 0 °C.
The water lowers the temperature at which the plants' cells freeze.
The spray blows away the cold air that settles over the field.
items.explain:
The passage states that water releases heat as it freezes (about 334 J per gram). This released heat keeps the plant tissue at about 0 °C, above the roughly −2 °C at which damage begins.

Freezing water gives off heat; it does not absorb it. The passage says nothing about the water changing the freezing point of plant cells or about the spray moving air.

items.prompt: Why is frost more likely on a clear night than on a cloudy night?
options: Clear skies allow cold to radiate down from space onto the plants.
Clouds produce heat that reaches the ground by conduction.
Without clouds, more heat radiates away from the ground and plants into space.
Clear nights always have strong winds that carry heat away by convection.
items.explain:
The ground and plants lose heat by giving off infrared radiation. Clouds absorb some of it and send part back down. On a clear night, nothing returns that energy, so more heat is lost and temperatures drop lower.

"Cold" is not a form of energy that flows; objects get colder by losing heat. Clouds do not touch the ground to conduct heat. The passage says frost is most likely on calm nights, not windy ones.

items.prompt: What was the truck's average speed from 40 minutes to 60 minutes, in kilometers per hour?
options: 52 km/h
72 km/h
84 km/h
156 km/h
items.explain:
Distance traveled: 52 km − 24 km = 28 km.
Time: 60 min − 40 min = 20 min = 20 ÷ 60 = 1/3 hour.
Speed = 28 km ÷ 1/3 h = 28 × 3 = 84 km/h.

52 km/h is the average speed for the whole hour (52 km ÷ 1 h). 72 km/h is the speed from 0 to 20 minutes (24 km in 1/3 h). 156 km/h comes from using the total distance, 52 km, instead of the 28 km traveled in this interval.

items.prompt: During which time interval was the truck stopped at the farm supply store?
options: 0 to 20 minutes
20 to 40 minutes
40 to 60 minutes
The truck did not stop during the first hour.
items.explain:
From 20 to 40 minutes, the distance stays at 24 km, so the line on the graph is flat (horizontal). A flat line on a distance-time graph means the object is not moving.

During the other intervals, the distance increases, so the truck was moving.

items.prompt: A farm uses a solar panel to run a small irrigation pump. The panel supplies the pump with 24 volts (V) and a current of 5 amperes (A). Electric power is found with P = V × I. How much electrical energy, in watt-hours (Wh), does the pump use if it runs for 3 hours?
options: 40 Wh
72 Wh
120 Wh
360 Wh
items.explain:
Step 1, power: P = 24 V × 5 A = 120 W.

Step 2, energy: energy = power × time = 120 W × 3 h = 360 Wh.

120 Wh is the power alone, the answer for just 1 hour. 40 Wh comes from dividing by 3 instead of multiplying. 72 Wh multiplies the voltage by the time and leaves out the current.

items.prompt: Weather forecasters use several kinds of electromagnetic waves: radio waves carry forecasts to farm radios, Doppler radar sends out microwaves to detect rain, satellites photograph clouds in visible light, and the daily ultraviolet (UV) index warns farmworkers about sunburn risk. Put these waves in order from longest wavelength to shortest wavelength.
items.explain:
In order of decreasing wavelength, the electromagnetic spectrum runs: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

So the order is radio waves → microwaves → visible light → ultraviolet rays.

A common mistake is reversing the order. Shorter wavelength means higher energy, which is why UV rays can damage skin while radio waves cannot.

items.prompt: Farmers sometimes test seeds by dropping them in water: healthy, solid seeds tend to sink, while hollow or damaged seeds float. A bean seed has a mass of 0.60 g and a volume of 0.50 cm3. The density of water is 1.0 g/cm3. Which statement is correct?
options: The seed's density is 1.2 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, so it sinks.
The seed's density is 1.2 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, so it floats.
The seed's density is 0.83 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, so it floats.
The seed's density is 0.83 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, so it sinks.
items.explain:
Density = mass ÷ volume = 0.60 g ÷ 0.50 cm3 = 1.2 g/cm3.

1.2 g/cm3 is greater than water's 1.0 g/cm3, so the seed sinks.

0.83 g/cm3 comes from dividing volume by mass (0.50 ÷ 0.60). An object floats only if its density is less than the liquid's, so a density of 1.2 g/cm3 cannot float in water.

items.prompt:
Which of these farm events are chemical changes?

Select two answers.
options: Corn stalks burning in a field fire, producing ash and smoke
Bacteria in a silo turning the sugars in chopped corn into acids
Water evaporating from an irrigation ditch
Wheat kernels being ground into flour
Ice on a water trough melting in the morning sun
items.explain:
In a chemical change, new substances form. Burning turns corn stalks into ash, smoke, carbon dioxide, and water vapor. Fermentation in a silo turns sugars into acids, which are different substances.

Evaporating, melting, and grinding are physical changes: the water is still water and the flour is still wheat, only in a different state or size.

items.prompt: Which conclusion about the period from 12 PM to 3 PM is best supported by the data?
options: Air pressure was rising, which often signals clear, calm weather ahead.
The temperature fell steadily, which shows that cold air had already arrived.
Rain fell every hour, which shows that the storm had already passed.
Air pressure was falling, which often signals that stormy weather is approaching.
items.explain:
From 12 PM to 3 PM, air pressure dropped from 1008 to 1006 to 1004 to 1003 hPa. Falling pressure often means a low-pressure system or front is approaching, bringing clouds and storms. Rain began by 3 PM, and the heaviest rain fell in the next hour.

Pressure was falling, not rising. The temperature stayed near 31–32 °C until 3 PM, so cold air had not yet arrived. No rain fell from 12 PM to 2 PM.

items.prompt: Which type of front most likely passed the farm, and when did it pass?
options: A cold front, between 3 PM and 4 PM
A warm front, between 3 PM and 4 PM
A cold front, between 12 PM and 1 PM
A warm front, between 5 PM and 6 PM
items.explain:
Between 3 PM and 4 PM, the temperature dropped sharply from 30 °C to 22 °C, the wind shifted from southwest to northwest, the pressure began rising after reaching its lowest value (1003 hPa), and the heaviest rain fell (18 mm). These are the signs of a cold front passing.

A warm front would bring warmer temperatures afterward, not a drop. From 12 PM to 1 PM the temperature rose, and from 5 PM to 6 PM conditions were already cool and steady.

items.prompt: The corn crop on this farm needs about 25 mm of water per week. The rain that fell during this afternoon supplied what percent of one week's need? Enter a whole number.
items.explain:
Total rainfall: 4 + 18 + 6 = 28 mm.

Percent = 28 ÷ 25 × 100 = 1.12 × 100 = 112%.

A common error is dividing the other way (25 ÷ 28 ≈ 89%). The part being compared (28 mm of rain) goes on top, and the weekly need (25 mm) is the whole. The answer is above 100% because the storm supplied more than a week's need.

items.prompt: Farmers in the Northern Hemisphere plant corn in spring so that it grows during the warm months of June, July, and August. Which statement best explains why these months are warmer in the Northern Hemisphere?
options: Earth is closest to the Sun in July.
Earth's tilted axis points the Northern Hemisphere toward the Sun, so it receives more direct sunlight and longer days.
The Sun gives off more energy during the Northern Hemisphere's summer.
Earth rotates more slowly in summer, so the days last longer everywhere on Earth.
items.explain:
Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis (about 23.5°). From June to August, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so sunlight strikes it more directly and days are longer. Both effects deliver more energy.

Earth is actually slightly farthest from the Sun in early July, so distance cannot explain summer. The Sun's output does not change with our seasons, and Earth's rotation speed does not change either. When it is summer in the Northern Hemisphere, it is winter in the Southern Hemisphere, which a change in the Sun or in distance could not explain.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about water used to irrigate a field.

Some of the irrigation water returns to the atmosphere when it {{0}} from the warm soil surface. Crop plants also release water vapor through their leaves in a process called {{1}}. High in the atmosphere, the water vapor cools and {{2}} into tiny droplets that form clouds.

options: evaporates
condenses
precipitates
infiltrates
respiration
transpiration
condensation
germination
evaporates
melts
condenses
sublimates

items.explain:
Evaporation changes liquid water into water vapor. Water vapor leaving plants through their stomata is transpiration. When water vapor cools, it condenses (changes back into liquid) to form cloud droplets.

Condensation is the reverse of evaporation, so it cannot describe water leaving the soil. Respiration releases energy from food; it is not the name for water loss from leaves. Infiltration is water soaking into the ground.

items.prompt: The sentences below come from a farm newsletter. Click the sentence that describes the region's climate rather than its weather.
spans: A thunderstorm dropped 40 mm of rain on the county yesterday afternoon.
This morning's low temperature was 3 °C, with patchy frost in low-lying fields.
Over the past 30 years, the county has averaged 180 frost-free days per year.
Winds gusted to 50 km/h during last night's storm.
Forecasters expect clear skies and light winds tomorrow.
items.explain:
Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular time and place. Climate is the average pattern of weather in a region over a long period, usually 30 years or more.

The sentence about the county averaging 180 frost-free days per year over the past 30 years describes a long-term average, so it describes climate. The other sentences describe conditions on a single day or night, which is weather.
